blocks: … the fortunes of men and the conditions of cities and peoples, as they change, turn out alike in smaller things and in greater, in peace and in war, since time leaves nothing as it is, but turns different people different ways, and towards the better too. And indeed those judge best of what happens in human affairs who do not take the changes of days and seasons hard; and those who lead in war and in camps, from the memory of what went before, keep each thing to what is most useful, and in the troubles that befall … of what has been recorded, both more recent and older … but towards those … among men, where there is no way out … for those who are strong against … to the one who shares in … so that it must be taken.

flags.accepted: Müller numbers Dexippus's fragments straight through his works: 1–2 are the History after Alexander, 3–16a the Chronica, so the Scythica starts at 17

blocks: From the works of Dexippus. The siege of Marcianopolis.

Marcianopolis: the people of the country say that the sister of the emperor Trajan gave the city her name. This city, then, the Scythians thought could be taken by storm. They held off from attacking it at once, but carried as many stones as they could up in front of the wall, so as to have them heaped up in piles, plentiful and ready to use; for they thought that in this way there would be great slaughter on the wall, and that, with the enemy busy guarding themselves rather than attacking, they would take the city easily. But the people in the town had long since prepared everything needed for a siege; and Maximus, a man of humble birth … who lived the life of a philosopher, and was ready at that time to show the deeds not only of a good general but of a good soldier, encouraged them all and urged them, whenever the enemy skirmished at close range, to hold back from fighting back, and to stand under the battlements and protect themselves, holding out their shields and whatever else could cover them and ward off the enemy's missiles.

When the barbarians thought they had enough stones ready, they poured round the wall all together, some hurling javelins, others pelting the men on the battlements with stones, and they kept up such a stream of missiles that in its unbroken fall it was like the thickest hail. The men inside the town protected themselves and the wall as well as they could, and held back from fighting back, as they had been ordered. When the barbarians had used up their store of stones to no great effect, and all the javelins they had, thrown by hand or shot from the bow, and their hope of taking the city without toil was spent, they lost heart, and when their generals called them back they went away and made camp not far from the city; for it was about sunset.

After a few days they came on again, stood round the wall and skirmished; and then Maximus told the men in the town that the moment to strike had come. So it was done. Encouraged by the barbarians' fruitless retreat the time before, they raised a shout and let fly stones and javelins, whatever they had. Since the barbarians stood packed close together, and, not expecting anything to come against them from above, were not well protected, the men from the town could not have missed even if they had wanted to, so great was the number of the enemy and so thick the volleys, and these thrown from a height. So the Scythians, hard pressed and unable to strike back at the Moesians, because of the battlements and the watch kept from the gates, gave up under the blows, and since they could hold out no longer, they withdrew having achieved nothing.

blocks: Decius, emperor of the Romans … had the Thracian force … fearing that something new might happen to the state of the empire … a letter … to go out against the enemy themselves … wanting … to lead … so that men acting no further … might not have the trial of an untimely eagerness … to come to … help. And the courier … of the emperor, carrying the … to Priscus, who … of the … had mostly conducted … in peace … the affairs of war; but the … and the war that was then … they reported. And when they had gathered … for the letter said this:

"That we long … men … safe in the sight of those who see … But since … going … acting … you would … to me; if indeed … why … if any of you should delay; for it is reported … that you are bold out of youth, not at the right time, and think that by this you will strike terror into the enemy, being untried in war, and so act more boldly than prudently in the absence of men to fight in front of you. Your attempt is not altogether blameworthy, since it is for a fine cause; and I would pray with you that in the trial too you may prove most useful. But I have observed that in war courage joined with experience is strong, and without it weak; and rashness without reasoning, joined with untimely daring, has brought men down. Best are those who know by understanding the difference in what will follow, rather than those who go into battle in passion. I urge you, then, not to look at the readiness of your resolve and the unsteadiness of the crowd and so give up the common safety; for in this way you will put your safety at risk for no need, and your mind will seem to be troubled rather than to hold, for the whole city, a well-laid plan for what will happen. The man who shrinks from the struggle at hand from cowardice and the man who rushes rashly into dangers that do not concern him, when he could keep his life in safety, are equally to blame. A man who trusts reasoning stands firmer than one who launches himself in the guise of ignorance (or, of spirit) against the uncertain turns of events. The chances of war either give daring to those who go out into danger from necessity, or, from a surplus of safety, give them the good sense that goes with security, so that they do nothing in fear, in haste rather than with forethought.

"Reckoning these things, do not go out to fight, alone and with no one to help you, against men who come on with a strong force, equipped with much cavalry and many heavy and light infantry, and moreover fearsome in their experience of war, terrible to look at in body, and, with the brandishing of their arms, their threats and the loudness of their shouting, most able to strike terror beforehand into those who first come against them. Do not run the risk against these men, when you can defend yourselves in safety from the walls. For hope seems to those who first go into battle a strong thing, and a great help towards success; but in the most famous cases it has been seen … when it fights against the truth. It is clear, I think, that even for those on equal terms it is most dangerous to run the risk alone and without a general; but to be led by a commander and to share the danger with others is safest both in planning and in action, since it allows easy correction by one's neighbour. It is better to win with another and have less glory than to fail by attempting alone without forethought. If help is far away, it is forgivable for men left on their own to do something rashly; but when men who are most at home in war, and have given proof of victory, are not far off, and moreover when you have, in the meantime, safety from danger in the strength of your walls, to do anything against the will of the commander, even if it turns out well, has never been free of reproach, both because of the disobedience to the man who gave the order, and because it was attempted with the risk of the danger uncertain.

"If anyone is aggrieved at being deprived of the pleasure of his suburbs and country houses, and of whatever adornments wealth gives, let him know that the pain will be brief and will be felt briefly, since it lies in buildings, and since we shall arrive before long, so as to prevent their utter destruction and to be able to restore them abundantly from the supplies for it; whereas he will not be able to heal the danger to his own life. So let him set lasting safety against the present vexation, and reckon thus: that the loss does not fall on everyone, but only on those who are able to bear it, whose wealth is great, and who can quickly make good what was taken even without our help. You must, then, give up this impulse, if you are not to act against yourselves and in opposition to your commander, and you must stay inside the walls. Expect us, who have not given up the common safety either in our preparations or in our resolve, to arrive within a few days with our force; and inside the walls we will see to what is needed to win the fight outside. That this promise is not far from the truth is shown already by what was done at Nicopolis, unless I am to be thought boastful. In the greatest struggles one must use as counsellors and helpers at once those who in earlier deeds have given clear proof of what is useful, experience of deeds and …"

blocks: From the works of Dexippus. The siege of Philippopolis.

Philippopolis: this city lies on the border between the land of the Thracians and that of the Macedonians, on the river Hebrus, and they say that its founder was Philip, son of Amyntas, king of the Macedonians, from whom the city took its name. The Scythians attacked it to besiege it as the most ancient and the greatest city there. They made war on it in this way. Holding their shields above their heads, to be under cover from what was thrown, they went round the city, looking for where it might be easy to cut off, or easy to scale with ladders where the walls were narrow or low. At first they made their attacks with skirmishing and archery; and the men above defended themselves stoutly wherever the enemy came near.

Then they tried the city again, having built ladders and engines. The engines were square frames of timber, contrivances like little houses; over them they stretched hides, so as to come up against the gates unharmed by anything thrown, holding their shields before them, and moving the engines on wheels and with levers. Some lifted long beams, sheathed in iron so as not to break in the attack, and tried to batter the wall; others set up ladders against it, some fixed upright, others on wheels, moving now one way and now another; and when these were brought up, they unfolded them with ropes tied to the tops of the ladders, so as to raise them and lay them against the walls. And some brought up wooden towers on wheels against the wall, so that when they came close they could cross from them on a level by throwing bridges across. Such was their abundance of engines.

But the Thracians held out against each of them. Some of the engines they smashed, men and all, with great stones the size of a wagonload; others they set on fire with torches and sulphur and pitch. Down the ladders they rolled cross-beams and stones, so that under the violent fall the shields of those bringing them up and the ladders themselves were broken in the assault. When the enemy gained nothing by their engines, they lost heart, and taking counsel how to make war, they resolved to heap up high mounds against the city, so that they could fight the enemy on a level. They heaped them up in this way. They carried together timber from the buildings round about, and, holding their shields before them, threw it into the ditch lengthwise and crosswise, however it fell. Having done this, they carried earth and every kind of material between the two edges of the ditch. And so they made the mound rise quickly.

When the Thracians saw what was being done, and that the mound was being raised against them like a counter-wall, they set up timbers, fastened planks to them, and raised a high screen on the wall. And besides this they contrived the following. At night they let down from the wall by ropes, at some quiet spot, a bold and brave man, and gave him to carry to the mound a lighted torch and a vessel holding pitch and sulphur and such things. He set fire to the timbers holding up the mound, and when they burned the mound collapsed all at once.

When the Scythians had the worst of it in this too, they resolved to kill the useless pack animals, and those of the captives who were suffering from sickness, or from age through the passing of time. Having killed them they threw them into the ditch and carried every kind of material over them. The bodies, by the third day, swelling up, gave no small height to the mound. But the Thracians cut through a part of the wall, as large as a narrow postern, and through it carried the earth over to their side every night. When the barbarians were at a complete loss in their plans, they resolved to withdraw. And this was the end of the siege for the Scythians.

blocks: "… and wars are decided by endurance rather than by numbers. We have no mean force (for we have gathered two thousand in all), and a very strong position, from which we must set out to harm the enemy, falling on them when they are scattered and laying ambushes on their routes. If we win in this way we shall gain strength, and we shall cause the enemy no small fear; and if they gather against us, we shall stand against them, having the strength of the position and this wood as no mean defence. The enemy, attacking from different directions against men they cannot fully see, will be thrown into confusion, and will not fight as they did before: they will break their ranks, not knowing where to shoot their arrows and javelins, and they will miss with what they throw and suffer still more harm from you. We, protected by the wood, shall shoot from a height, taking aim from above, and we shall be safer for doing harm and not easy to harm. As for fighting hand to hand, if it should come to that too, we must reckon this: that the greatest dangers give the greatest eagerness, that resistance is readier when there is no other way to safety, and that much has turned out beyond hope when men are forced to it by a desperate need and defend what is worth the effort in hope of vengeance. For there is no one who could have greater cause for anger than we, since our families and our city are held by the enemy. And those who serve with them unwillingly, under compulsion, would join in attacking them when they learned of our approach, in hope of their own freedom.

"I learn also that the emperor's fleet is not far off, to come to our aid; it would be best to join it and attack together. And besides this I believe that we shall draw the Greeks too to the same eagerness. I myself, not out of danger nor in better fortune than you, set out on this, longing for honour and taking the risk, wanting to keep what is most precious and not to let the city's standing come to an end in me. And I urge you to think this way. Death comes upon all men to end their lives, but in struggles for one's country it brings the finest prize and everlasting fame. And if, after what has been said, anyone is struck down by the fall of the city and has lost heart because of it, let him know that most cities have been taken by the enemy by ambush … and, deprived of those who stood against them … to attack the barbarian host. And … we shall join together against the one who resists … they will use the passage all together … we should be able; we shall withdraw to the high ground in safety … we shall attack them as they …, and in this the enemy's difficulties will be our gain.

"It is likely too that fortune will stand with us; for our cause is most just, since we are defending ourselves against those who wronged us first, and the divine power for the most part decides human affairs in this way, being most ready to lessen misfortunes and to help towards better things. It is a fine thing to make known our ancestral bearing, to become ourselves an example of courage and freedom to the Greeks, and to share in an ever-remembered glory among the living and among those to come, showing by our deeds that even in misfortune the spirit of the Athenians has not been beaten. Taking our children and those dearest to us as the watchword of the war, and the saving of them, let us form up for the fight, calling on the gods who watch over us to help us."
So he spoke; and the Athenians were greatly strengthened by what was said (for it was well able to bring them to resist), and on this they asked him to lead them.
The eagerness of those who choose the best course is praised, even if the deed does not follow.

To a man who holds command, the failure of the whole is more painful than to each man his own hurt; for to the private man the fortune of what happens is limited to himself, but to the commander comes the feeling of all that has befallen. It is no small weight, to be persuaded that others think alike; and it is likely … with goodwill. And I find I can take courage from the same things from which the difficulty began.

Dexippus, speaking to the Greeks, says: "And let it not occur to anyone that … of your safety … late … For I knew what was of common benefit … another, and to do … to blame, whose task it is to consider what will be useful and … a man who holds his office by right and governs best, by persuasion …"

blocks: When he (Claudius) passed to the gods and to the stars, Quintillus, his brother, … took the empire. Under him the barbarians who had survived laid waste Anchialus and tried to take Nicopolis too; but they were crushed by the courage of the provincials. Quintillus, because of the shortness of his time, could do nothing worthy of the empire. For on the seventeenth day, because he had shown himself stern and serious towards the soldiers and promised to be a true emperor, he was killed in the same way as Galba and Pertinax. And Dexippus, indeed, does not say that Quintillus (Claudius, the common text) was killed, but only that he died; yet he did not add "of disease", so that he seems to have been in doubt.
text: When he (Claudius) passed to the gods and to the stars, Quintillus, his brother, … took the empire. Under him the barbarians who had survived laid waste Anchialus and tried to take Nicopolis too; but they were crushed by the courage of the provincials. Quintillus, because of the shortness of his time, could do nothing worthy of the empire. For on the seventeenth day, because he had shown himself stern and serious towards the soldiers and promised to be a true emperor, he was killed in the same way as Galba and Pertinax. And Dexippus, indeed, does not say that Quintillus (Claudius, the common text) was killed, but only that he died; yet he did not add "of disease", so that he seems to have been in doubt.

blocks: From the works of Dexippus. The siege of Side.

The Scythians were besieging Side; this city is one of those in Lycia. Since there was abundant provision of every kind inside the wall, and a host of men who set to the work with no slackness, they made engines and brought them up to the wall. The defenders held out against these too, letting down every kind of obstacle. Besides this they built wooden towers of the same height as the wall and moved them on wheels so as to stand close by. Some of the towers were covered with iron beaten thin and fixed over much of the timber, others with hides and whatever could not be set on fire.

The men in the town contrived this in reply. They set up large upright planks where the enemy were going to bring up their engines, and fixed cross-timbers and scaffolding to them, and in the middle of the planks they made openings large enough to take a man up to the chest, so that, standing higher than the towers, they could defend themselves from above. Having done this, they let down from the top, hanging all round, cloaks and fleeces, so that such screens would not easily catch fire, and by their softness would hold whatever stuck in them, not resisting the force of the blow. When both sides had made trial of these devices, and there had been a hard fight, since the time spent was fruitless for the Scythians and nothing went forward towards their hopes, they withdrew.

blocks: When Aurelian had defeated the Juthungian Scythians outright, and had killed many of them as they fled at the crossing of the Ister, those who were left came to seek a truce and sent an embassy. They decided to ask for peace not in an over-fearful way, as though struck down by their defeat, so that they might still receive the money that used to come to them from the Romans, and the enemy might not feel altogether free of danger.

When Aurelian, the emperor of the Romans, learned that the embassy of the Juthungi had arrived, he said he would deal the next day with the matters they had come about, and drew up his soldiers as if for battle, to strike terror into the enemy. When his arrangements were well in order, he went up onto a high platform and stood above them, wearing purple, and made the whole army stand around him in one formation. Beside him stood all the officials entrusted with any command, all of them on horseback. Behind the emperor were the standards of the picked army: these are golden eagles, images of the emperors, and the names of the legions shown in golden letters, all of which were displayed raised high on silver-plated poles. When everything had been arranged like this, he bade the Juthungi come forward. They were amazed at what they saw, and for a long while stood in silence. When the emperor gave them leave to speak, they said this through an interpreter:

"We do not hasten to peace because we are struck down beyond reason by the misfortune that befell us at this moment, nor because we lack strength, nor because we are untried in war, using a show of weakness for our own advantage alone. No: we have so great an abundance for war, in numbers and in strength, that with a very small part of our force we attacked the cities on the Ister and have taken almost the whole of Italy. We took the field with forty thousand horse, and these not mixed or weak, but pure Juthungi, whose fame in cavalry fighting is great. And we bring infantry twice the strength of our cavalry, and in these too we do not overshadow the invincibility of our army by mixing in others. Being able, even so, to contend with such an army, we do not mean to come to argument about our misfortune. It is not because we were defeated outright, but because of the uncertainty of how things will turn out, that we prefer peace to war, supposing that you too would think it well, now that the chance is offered, to come to terms with the Juthungi after the earlier quarrel, since there has long been a mutual trust between our two peoples in keeping the peace; and for its sake both sides ought now to end this present thoughtless quarrel and return to what is older and more profitable.

"In the war, too, we did not plunder by raids as much as we could, but were content with gathering enough for our supplies; and until the battle we spent the time quietly, only drawing up our own force against you as you came on with yours. This is what we are now ready to do; and in this way your side will be safer against every danger, and when the greatest armies come together, no other force at all will be thought a match for us. If anyone, elated by success in the war, makes light of the agreement, let him know that he grows bold on a thing that is not secure, and that it is dangerous in every way for men who have been overcome by an apparent good fortune, and turned aside by fortune's present height, to hang on hopes of better things alone, and in such folly to disregard the change to the other side and refuse an alliance offered at the right time. For greater armies are apt, at first, elated by confidence in their own strength and using very little forethought, to go into battle despising their opponents, and through lack of care to come off worse for the most part; while those who meet what has come suddenly and against expectation with safe reasoning, and use their abundance of strength steadily, become very hard for their opponents to fight. With such a hope we too, though we first divided our force in two, and at the river suffered mostly from fortune rather than from your courage, are not taken by surprise; rather, joined now with forethought for the future, we cannot be withstood by you. For these reasons it is best for you to choose through peace the benefits of concord, to make common cause with us in the affairs of war, and, strengthened by our alliance, to have the advantage over those who attack you. If you decide to do this, it is just that we should receive all that used to come to us from you in gifts of gold, coined and uncoined, and of silver, as a pledge of firm friendship. If you refuse, we shall fight as enemies defending ourselves, as best we can."

To this the emperor of the Romans replied as follows: "If you had set out your intention plainly about what your embassy is for, you would not have made the answer difficult for us who received your speech. But since what you have said is put together for a fine show, while in fact it is the opposite, since you speak now of peace and now again threaten war, and seem to confuse each with the other, it is doubtful for us too what we must answer first so as not to go wrong. Something, however, remains to be decided from what is before us: we must take these two arguments apart and meet both. If you are offering peace pure and simple, why must you mention a demand for money? And yet even in this the victors need not hurry their decision to refuse or consent. But if you still think that your advantage, and the gains of war, are the purpose of the agreement, and have come, though defeated, as if to demand tribute from us, thinking that we pursue at all costs the pleasure of ease that peace gives, then hold to the same attempt as before, and do not, holding out the end of the war as a kindness, ask a reward for yielding, making the present invitation to friendship bought and not willing.

"For you will not frighten us, who are not untried in war, with the numbers of the force you have boasted of so much; nor will you go home safely laden with the wealth of Italian plunder. Your infantry forces are plain to see, and your cavalry no less, and we shall stand against them as best we can. For we dare with safety and withdraw with forethought, using reasoning as our guide in everything, which gives strength its greatest firmness, and having outstanding experience in the work of war. You come on hastily, and, failing in your deeds because you did not consider what you were going into, you repent, suffering in practice the harm of rashness. For those who are carried into action by heat, not by understanding, must miss what is best. Your attempts are quick, and your regrets come soon after. And there is nothing at all to wonder at, as is likely, in our having opponents of unlike character and of differing purpose, and in your living with ignorance and we with reason, by which most of all the fewer come to overcome the more, trusting understanding before strength.

"That the greater numbers who go into battle without thought are brought down the worse, you learn by the test of deeds rather than by boastful pretence of words, if you look at what the Scythians suffered; for we shall speak with the clearest proofs, and not without witnesses. These, with an army of three hundred thousand scattered over both continents, were defeated by us with all their force, and they left the victors splendid memorials of their own courage, whose glory we shall keep for ever, now and hereafter, running alongside time. And the disasters of the Alamanni … made their repentance quicker than the rashness with which they threw themselves into the attempt, and soon. And we, for the wrongs you have done us, do not think the punishment you have suffered is enough, unless we also cross the Ister and fill up our anger in your own territory, since you wronged us first. For you raised against us, during a truce, a war without a herald; you could not name any wrong as against men who had wronged you first, but, lifted up by certain desires and hopes, by which a thoughtless multitude is carried away, you took to arms and war. So we do not think it beyond expectation that help will come to us from the divine power too, since we did not dishonour the law of truces, while the Juthungi came against us by an unjust road and held oaths and every pledge of good faith of little account.

"Taking the future from our earlier successes, we judge not unreasonably that besides what has been said, what is to come will be good. For hope of success brings boldness, and the opposite brings fear. Using reasoning as our guide in action, we do not accept opinions about what will happen without testing them, and in present things, like men who are athletes in the noblest dangers, we are not dismayed by the hardships of war, from which the gain we hope for is not small, and greater than the trouble. For your multitude is weakest both in body and in spirit. It is shut in within the Rhône (or the Po, Valesius) and within our borders; and, held fast by scarcity of food and other hardship, it is already in the midst of some sufferings and about to meet others. And being worn out in advance by constant toil, it will become less daring, and will let us deal with it as we please without a fight, as men exhausted by long delay. So for you everything is plainly at risk, and your request for peace is put together as a cover for fear, so that you may hide your own dread. Why should we accept it, when we may very well, since you are shut off on every side from the road home and caught as it were within the gates, treat you well or ill, as our intentions towards you may be?"
When the emperor had said this, the Juthungi were dismayed, and since nothing was going as they had hoped, they gave up all hope of a truce and went back to their own people.

In the time of Aurelian, the Vandals, defeated outright by the Romans, sent an embassy to the Romans about ending the war and making terms. After the emperor and the barbarians had said much to each other, the meeting broke up; but the next day the whole body of the Roman soldiers was gathered again, and when the emperor asked them what seemed better to them in the present situation, they judged it best to keep the good fortune they had with forethought for the safety of what they held, and, showing their wish by a shout, all of them went for ending the war. So these were agreed in this way. The kings and rulers of the barbarians, coming as had been arranged, gave hostages from among themselves, not of second rank in standing and fortune. For both kings gave their sons as hostages without hesitating, and others with them not far behind in standing. And on these terms they came to an agreement, and the truce was made.

From this time two thousand Vandal horsemen fought as allies of the Romans, some chosen from the multitude and enrolled for the alliance, others taking up the service of their own free will. The rest of the Vandal host made its way home, the Roman ruler providing them with a market as far as the Ister. Most of it got through unharmed; but those who, breaking the truce, scattered freely to gather plunder were all killed by the commander of the foreign troops, and they were no fewer than five hundred. For since they were travelling through friendly country, and were elated with confidence by the peace made with the Romans, they broke away from the whole column and made sudden raids, with their leader's consent, and did no little harm to the country. And for this deed the man who did it was shot down with arrows at the emperor's order … The rest of the Vandals scattered and went home.

The emperor of the Romans sent most of his infantry and cavalry to Italy. And after a few days he himself, taking with him his own company of companions, the ruler's bodyguard, the Vandal allies, and the boys given him as hostages, marched to Italy in haste, because the Juthungi had come again.
